narratives.Description: perf(hooks): the write path spends 5.8s on a duplicate forge call and 11s on redundant git spawns, and the host kills it
narratives.Overview:
## Summary

The agent-hook mutation write path takes ~18 s and is killed by the host's effective 5 s budget, so **an authorized write is denied by timeout**. The hook computes `allow`; the operator still cannot write or dispatch.

Two costs dominate. Five git subprocesses, four redundant (~11.3 s). And a **live forge call on the authorization path** (~5.8 s) that is a duplicate of a guarantee enforced elsewhere, discards its own answer, and fails closed against #3422.

Recut after three critique rounds. Round 1 bound a git-memoization remedy; round 2 measured it insufficient; round 3 (N=3 panel) established what the forge call actually does. Several claims in earlier revisions were false and are withdrawn below.

## Measured

Global `@deftai/directive` 0.107.0 — what `deft-hook` executes; rebuilding the checkout changes nothing.

| Component | Cost |
|---|---|
| five git children | 11,315 ms |
| `where ghx` + `ghx api repos/.../issues/<N>` | 124 + 5,860 ms |
| Node startup, JSON/state, gated step, dispatch | 709 ms |
| **total, verdict `allow / write-ready`** | **18,008 ms** |

Memoization alone: **7,763 ms** — still over. Deleting all remaining git children would still leave 4,598 ms. Memoization **plus** no forge call: **4,108 ms**, the only measured variant inside budget.

> **Caveat under active investigation.** `resolveBinary` prefers `ghx`, and one measurement put `ghx` at 1,810–3,350 ms where plain `gh` cost 683–708 ms on the same endpoint. If that holds, every latency figure here is inflated by the proxy. It does not change the remedy — the forge call is removable on correctness grounds regardless of speed — but treat the magnitudes as provisional. Tracked at #3737.

## The forge call is a duplicate that throws away its own answer

This is the round-3 finding and it decides the issue.

**Drift is common.** Replaying the exported detector across the corpus: **307 of 595** briefs with a resolvable origin are stale — **51.6%**, median lag 43 minutes. So the check is not firing rarely.

**But the hot path discards the result.** `inspectActiveScope` walks active briefs in sort order, returns ready as soon as any one passes, and keeps a `scope.path` unrelated to the file being written. Measured live: **two of three briefs in `xbrief/active/` fail preflight on origin staleness while the write gate still allows**, rescued by whichever brief sorts first.

**And the guarantee already lives elsewhere, per brief.** #3363 ("origin GitHub updates after ingest are not fail-closed at activate") placed this tripwire at `xbrief:preflight`. The hook instance is a **second copy**.

So removing it deletes redundancy. It does not relocate a guarantee and opens no staleness gap, because the hot path provides no per-brief guarantee to lose.

## It also contradicts #3422, and the tree already decided this the other way

The call **fails closed on any fetch error**. With a simulated 503, all three active briefs returned exit 1 — denying every in-repo write and every spawn. Three files away, `preflight-cache/evaluate.ts` fails **open** on the sibling forge probe, with an explicit `#3738 / #3422` comment marking that as deliberate.

Same authorization path, opposite postures, one chosen and one not.

## What to build

1. **Remove the live origin-freshness call from `inspectActiveScope`.** `preflight/evaluate.ts` already exposes `skipOriginFreshness`; `hooks/scope.ts` simply never passes it. No boundary decision is required — the boundary is `xbrief:preflight`.
2. **Memoize the redundant git spawns.** Necessary, not sufficient, unchanged from round 1.
3. **Replace the acceptance criterion.** A child-process count would go green while the host still kills the hook. Acceptance must exercise the **host-observed path against the effective timeout**, where "effective" is the minimum across all loaded registrations.

If a hot-path freshness signal is still wanted later, the triage cache already holds `updated_at` for 1,352 entries: local read and parse measured **0.090 ms**, producing the **identical verdict on all three active briefs today**, with its staleness window already governed by `cache_fresh` (24 h TTL plus drift probe). That is a follow-up, not part of this change.

## Budget facts — corrected

Earlier revisions of this issue asserted, as verified, that the 5 s budget was "our own number in our own deposits" and that the Cursor `preToolUse` matchers were themselves 5 s. **Both are false.**

- All four `.cursor/hooks.json` `preToolUse` entries are **`timeout: 30`**, deliberately raised from 5 under #3246. `CURSOR_TOOL_BEFORE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30` in source carries a comment describing exactly this failure mode.
- Only the **nested** Claude / Grok / Codex deposits are 5 (`NESTED_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`).
- Cursor imports the nested Claude deposit and enforces the **minimum**, which is the sole source of the 5 s constraint.

The false claim had been used to weaken #3739. It does not — it strengthens it.

Root cause of the error, recorded so it is not repeated: the deposits use **two schemas**. Cursor is flat (`hooks.preToolUse[].timeout`); Claude and Codex are nested (`hooks.PreToolUse[].hooks[].timeout`). A reader written for one shape silently returns nothing on the other.

## Withdrawn from earlier revisions

- That memoizing git spawns alone brings the path within budget — measured insufficient at 7,763 ms.
- That the freshness boundary needed deciding before implementation — it already exists at `xbrief:preflight`.
- That origin freshness "almost never fires" — it fires 51.6% of the time.
- The two budget claims above.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `inspectActiveScope` performs no network I/O on the authorization path
- [ ] Redundant git subprocesses on the write path are memoized within a dispatch
- [ ] The host-observed `tool.before` path renders a verdict inside the effective budget, measured end to end rather than by child-process count
- [ ] Acceptance states the effective budget as the minimum across loaded registrations, not the value in any single deposit
- [ ] No regression: the gate still denies what it denied before, and `xbrief:preflight` still enforces origin freshness per brief
- [ ] CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]` entry

## Out of scope

- **The OR-fold in `inspectActiveScope`** — returning ready on any passing candidate with an unrelated `scope.path`. Whether that is a defect or a deliberately coarse "are you in a story at all" gate is **unestablished**, and file-level coverage is `verify:scope-provenance`'s job. Removing the freshness call must not be mistaken for having settled it.
- **Raising the nested 5 s budget** — #3739. Correct on its own terms and complementary, but it does not make this change unnecessary: per-write forge I/O is wrong at any budget.
- **`ghx` being preferred by `resolveBinary`, and its latency** — #3737.
- The `cache_fresh` forge-error fail-open decided on #3738.

Refs #3739, #3737, #3738, #3422, #3363, #3246, #3156.

## Stop 1 — triage write-back

Accepted `ae116884`. Chip: `design-critique:mechanism-shaped` — the issue names a specific mechanism (per-call `verifySessionRitual` on the `tool.before` path, deliberately non-cacheable agent-hook probing) with a code citation and measured latencies, not a symptom report.

The original numbers were taken while a **broken `ghx.exe`** was on PATH — it cannot start at all on this machine (`ghx --version` returns `0xC0000142` / `STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED`). Since `resolveBinary` prefers `ghx` over `gh` on mere PATH presence, that had to be excluded as a confound before spending critic budget.

Re-measured with `ghx` removed from PATH:

| Probe | ghx on PATH | ghx off PATH |
|---|---|---|
| `tool.before`, Write payload | 11.2 / 11.2 / 11.3s | **11.6 / 11.4 / 11.3s** |
| `verify:session-ritual --tier=gated` | 8.9 / 8.8s | **8.9 / 8.0s** |

The confound is excluded. The issue's numbers stand.

(The broken `ghx` is a separate, unrelated defect being filed on its own — it independently breaks `pr:watch`, `issue:ingest`, `triage:accept` and `cache:fetch-all` with an opaque empty-stderr failure. It is **not** part of this issue and critics should not treat it as in scope.)

## Stop 2 — variant selection

- **charter:** open critique
- **spend:** N≥3 (panel permission used)

**Why this charter.** The issue's mechanism claim is measured and cited, but the question the operator asked is *what are the options* — the remedy space, not the diagnosis. An open critique is the right charter for that. No refutation target is named, so the refutation row does not apply.

**Why this spend.** Both panel-permission conditions hold independently:

- *Genuinely open solution space.* At least four non-equivalent remedies are live and they trade off differently: cache the ritual verdict with event-based invalidation; evaluate at `sessionStart` only and keep `tool.before` to cheap checks; fail **open** on timeout while keeping fail-closed for real denials; or bound the live probe and report which sub-check overran. These are not variations on one design.
- *High blast radius.* The change sits on the fail-closed write path for **every consumer**, covering `Edit` / `Write` / `MultiEdit` / `StrReplace` / `Delete` / `ApplyPatch`. Getting it wrong either taxes every edit or weakens a security gate.

Per the Stop 2 evaluation rule, panel permission grants N≥3 without changing the charter, and the mechanism-shaped default of N=1 is a default rather than a ceiling.

### Known tension the panel should weigh

The non-cacheable probe is **deliberate**, not an oversight. The source comment states the intent plainly:

> Mutation dispatch is a live gated boundary: active verification reruns non-cacheable agent-hook readiness instead of trusting persisted success.

So "just cache it" has to answer why trusting a persisted pass is safe here, when the author explicitly decided it was not. Any remedy that caches must say what it gives up.

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-25T20:33:41Z)

model: gpt-5.6-sol-medium

## 1. The measured tax is real, but the stated expensive mechanism is not — `blocks-the-design`

**Evidence.** At dispatch SHA `71bf82162dd52fb429ec89997f20625255384ab4`, `inspectMutationGates` calls `verifySessionRitual(... tier: "gated")` on each non-exempt direct write/spawn (`packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts:862-877`). However, that verifier does **not** rerun the full gated ceremony: green `doctor` and `cache_fresh` steps are skipped; only `agent_hooks` is deliberately rerun (`packages/core/src/session/verify-session-ritual.ts:579-646`), followed by the active-CLI check and final state evaluation. More importantly, `evaluateAgentHookReadiness` explicitly skips the live probe in this maintainer source checkout (`packages/core/src/verify-env/agent-hook-readiness.ts:113-172`). I reproduced that exact result:

- `deft verify:hooks-installed --scope=agent --live` → `agent hook readiness skipped: maintainer source checkout`
- the persisted `gated_steps.agent_hooks.message` records the same skip
- nevertheless, a Write `tool.before` took 6.379s and direct gated verification took 4.368s; Shell `git status --short` took 0.840s

So the issue's latency observation is directionally confirmed, but its claim that the measured maintainer cost is caused by live-probing all four hosts is contradicted by the dispatch-SHA code and recorded runtime state.

**Concrete failure mode.** A remedy that optimizes or caches only the four-host live probe can leave most of the synchronous per-write cost intact (CLI startup, active-CLI validation, git/state work), while appearing to have fixed the named cause. Consumer and maintainer profiles may also have different dominant costs.

**Disposition consequence.** The issue cannot bind with “the non-cacheable live probe accounts for essentially all cost.” Reframe the defect as “the active gated verifier is on every mutation boundary,” then require a component profile for (a) maintainer skip, (b) consumer with one enabled host, and (c) consumer with all enabled hosts before selecting a remedy.

## 2. A discontinuous HEAD change does not inherit the cold ceremony — `blocks-the-design`

**Evidence.** `verifySessionRitual` first calls `evaluateLoadedState(... tier: "quick", rebindForwardHead: true)` (`verify-session-ritual.ts:579-598`). If the recorded HEAD is not an ancestor, `evaluateLoadedState` returns `code: 1` immediately with the cold-*recovery instruction* (`:306-327`). The verifier exits before any gated entrypoint. If the move is forward, it merely rebinds `git_head` and continues. The hook never invokes `session:ready` or `session:start`; those 48–57s cold-ceremony measurements are a different command path. Repository tests independently lock immediate discontinuity denial (`packages/core/src/session/branches.test.ts:431-449,481-483`).

**Concrete failure mode.** Correlating a post-merge 30s host timeout with “the hook inherited a 48–57s cold path” sends the design toward HEAD invalidation or a larger timeout even though the code either rebinds a forward move or denies a discontinuity before the expensive gated loop. The observed timeout may be real, but this mechanism does not explain it.

**Disposition consequence.** Keep “post-merge timeout” as an unverified reproduction target. Reproduce the exact transition (old/new SHA and ancestry result), capture whether Directive emitted any decision before Cursor killed it, and time each verifier phase. Do not use the cold `session:ready` duration to size or explain `tool.before`.

## 3. The omitted existing mechanism is the strongest baseline — `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** The code already has `inspectSessionRitual`, documented specifically as “Read-only ritual-state inspection for host hooks” and “A PreToolUse decision must be a probe, not a hidden `doctor` / cache-refresh mutation boundary” (`verify-session-ritual.ts:424-495`). It validates worktree, HEAD continuity, staleness, quick steps, and recorded gated steps without executing or rewriting them. Separately, `session:ready` already forces `agent_hooks` once, and init/update run readiness after depositing hooks (`content/contracts/agent-hook-readiness.md:49-58`).

**Concrete failure mode.** Designing a new session cache and event-invalidation protocol duplicates an existing state inspector, introduces more shared mutable state, and creates invalidation races across concurrent agents/worktrees.

**Disposition consequence.** Add an explicit baseline option: use `inspectSessionRitual` on the synchronous mutation path; keep live functional readiness at deposit/update and explicit `session:ready`; if between-boundary drift must be detected, add a cheap registration/shim fingerprint and rerun the live probe only when that evidence changes. This keeps occupancy, scope, intent, authz, and runtime-authority checks per call.

## 4. The four listed directions are axes, not four competing designs — `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** “Cache” versus “sessionStart only” chooses validation placement/invalidation. “Fail open on timeout” chooses authority semantics. “Bound and report the overrun” chooses budget and observability. They can be combined, so presenting them as alternatives obscures the actual decision.

**Concrete failure mode.** A successor may choose one bullet and silently leave the other two decisions unspecified—for example, cache readiness but retain an outer host timeout that still produces an opaque denial.

**Disposition consequence.** Characterize options on three independent axes: (1) synchronous evidence—inspect persisted state, fingerprint-triggered probe, or unconditional live probe; (2) invalidators—compact, worktree/HEAD, policy/deposit/shim fingerprint; (3) deadline result—explicit allow, explicit policy deny, or explicit readiness-unavailable deny rendered before Cursor's 30s kill. Compare complete combinations, not bullets.

## 5. Fail-open-on-timeout is unsafe on this authority boundary — `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** This hook protects direct writes and implementation spawns and shares a host timeout with concurrent work. A timeout can be induced by load/process starvation, including swarm concurrency; it is not evidence that occupancy, scope, intent, authz, or write-fence policy would have allowed the operation. Cursor's outer `failClosed` timeout is crude, but changing it to fail open makes resource exhaustion an authorization bypass.

**Concrete failure mode.** An untrusted repository or concurrent workload that keeps the verifier past its deadline gains writes/spawns without a policy verdict. That converts availability failure into authority escalation.

**Disposition consequence.** Remove general fail-open from the safe remedy set. The synchronous authorization path must be bounded enough to emit an explicit `readiness-unavailable` deny before the host deadline. Only diagnostics proven independent of authorization may time out open.

**Road not taken / steelman.** Fail-open is strongest when the check is purely health telemetry and denying destroys recoverability. It would flip my verdict only after the design separates all mutation-authority checks from that telemetry and demonstrates that timeout cannot skip any occupancy/scope/intent/authz/write-fence decision.

## 6. Shell is a routed but deliberately incomplete recovery channel — `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** Cursor deposits a fail-closed Shell matcher too (`packages/core/src/init-deposit/agent-hooks.ts:270-295`). In the dispatcher, unclassifiable Shell commands bypass `inspectMutationGates` and return `shell-op-unclassifiable`; recognized destination forms reach mutation gates only when `runtimeAuthority.shellDestForms === "enforce"` (`dispatcher.ts:1064-1121,1341-1346`). Thus Shell is not unhooked. Rather, common recovery commands—and many arbitrary shell writes—fall through a best-effort classifier.

**Concrete failure mode.** Calling Shell “exempt” or “incidental” hides both sides of the contract: it is the practical recovery route, but it is also a broad mutation bypass if treated as equivalent to direct-write enforcement.

**Disposition consequence.** State the invariant explicitly: recovery must remain non-recursive and available, while Shell classification is not proof of complete write interception. Test named recovery commands under stale/missing/drifted hook state; do not claim the direct-write gate covers Shell-authored files.

## Measurement note — `footnote`

My warm numbers were lower than the issue's 11s sample but still operationally material. The difference reinforces the need for phase-level distributions rather than weakening the existence of the per-write tax.

**Bottom line:** retain the issue, but recut it from “live hook probing plus cold HEAD timeout” into a synchronous-boundary design: cheap state inspection and policy authorization per mutation, readiness re-probed only on evidence change/explicit lifecycle boundaries, and an explicit fail-closed unavailable verdict before the host timeout.

## Parent correction — two of this issue's mechanism claims are refuted, verified independently

Posted after id ceiling `5416346836`. Out of envelope for the two round-1 siblings still running; recorded now because the issue body currently asserts a mechanism I can no longer support.

Critic B (`5416398786`) raised both as `blocks-the-design`. I re-derived each rather than accept them.

### 1. The cost is not the four-host live probe — the live probe does not run here

The body claims the per-write cost comes from live-probing all four host registrations. In this checkout the probe is **skipped outright**:

```
$ deft verify:hooks-installed --scope=agent --live
✓ deft agent hook readiness skipped: maintainer source checkout;
  consumer hook deposit is not applicable.
```

So whatever the ~11s is, it is not that. My attribution was wrong: I reasoned from the source comment about non-cacheable readiness to the conclusion that the probe dominates the cost, without checking whether the probe executes at all on the path I was timing.

Consequence: **a remedy that caches or optimises the live probe could ship, measure clean here, and leave the real per-write cost untouched.** The remaining cost is CLI startup plus active-CLI validation plus git/state work, and it has not been apportioned.

### 2. A discontinuous HEAD does not inherit the cold ceremony

The body claims a merge stales the ritual and the next write inherits the 48-57s cold path. It does not. `verifySessionRitual` runs a quick precheck first and returns on any non-zero code before reaching the gated work:

```ts
// verify-session-ritual.ts:579-598
const precheck = evaluateLoadedState(projectRoot, state, { tier: "quick", rebindForwardHead: true });
if (precheck.code !== 0) {
  return { code: precheck.code, message: precheck.message, ..., recoveryTier: precheck.recoveryTier };
}
```

A discontinuity produces an **immediate deny carrying a cold-recovery instruction**. It does not execute a cold ceremony. The hook never invokes `session:ready`, so my 48-57s figures — which came from `session:ready` — describe a different command path entirely.

I conflated two separate events I experienced minutes apart: a `timed out after 30s` block, and a later fast deny reading *"stale because git HEAD changed discontinuously … full cold ceremony required."* The second is an instruction to run a cold ceremony, not evidence that one ran. Reading the recovery text as the cause is the error.

### What this leaves standing, and what it does not

**Stands.** The per-write tax is real and reproduced by two independent measurements. Mine: 11.2-11.6s for a Write payload, 8.0-8.9s for the gated verifier alone, 0.5s for Shell — stable across a control run with the broken `ghx` removed from PATH. Critic B's: 6.379s Write, 4.368s gated, 0.840s Shell. Both confirm a material synchronous cost on every mutation; the spread between them is itself a finding, since it suggests load sensitivity.

**Does not stand.** The named cause, and the post-merge causal chain.

**Now unexplained.** What actually consumed 30s at the moment of the block. That is a reproduction target, not a conclusion. The load sensitivity implied by the two measurement sets is the more promising lead, and it is consistent with B's point that a timeout is an availability failure rather than a policy verdict.

I will not recut the body until the round closes and the synthesis is verified. Flagging now so no one builds against the refuted mechanism in the interim.


### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-25T20:35:49Z)

Round 1, fresh, open critique. Input ceiling honored: issue body + comment 5416346836 only. SHA at dispatch matches `git rev-parse HEAD` = `71bf82162dd52fb429ec89997f20625255384ab4`. Live hook on this machine is global `@deftai/directive@0.95.0` (`deft-hook` → `hook-bin.js`); that published dispatcher still calls `verifySessionRitual` and still has the non-cacheable comment. #480: no embedded instructions in the in-envelope text. ghx-off-PATH for every GitHub-adjacent and hook probe.

## 1. The merge-timeout story cannot bind `blocks-the-design`

**Evidence.** `verifySessionRitual` (gated, mutation) runs `evaluateLoadedState` as a *quick* precheck *before* any gated entrypoint. A non-ancestor HEAD move returns immediately with `headDriftRecoveryMessage()` / `recoveryTier: "cold"` and never calls `runGatedStep` (`packages/core/src/session/verify-session-ritual.ts` `evaluateLoadedState` + the gated precheck). `inspectMutationGates` then denies `ritual-not-ready`. It does not invoke `session:ready` or `session:start`. Unit coverage already locks the deny: reset-off-pin → code 1 + "discontinuously" (`verify-session-ritual.test.ts`).

HEAD moves are not one class. Forward moves (`gitIsAncestor(old, new)`) rebind under `rebindForwardHead: true` and continue. Only a non-ancestor move (rebase, reset, checkout to a divergent tip) stales. A same-branch merge or fast-forward pull is the forward case.

`session:ready` at 48–57s is a *recovery command*, not the hook's stale-state evaluator. I did not re-run that command (I am not refuting the 48–57s figure). I am refuting the claim that the next Write *inherits that ceremony inside `tool.before`* and therefore blows the 30s timeout.

**Failure mode.** A successor lean that treats "merge ⇒ next write times out" as the defect will size timeout, fail-open, or cold-path budgets against a path the hook does not run. The merge incident, if it really printed the discontinuous sentence, was a *fast deny until cold re-arm*. The observed `timed out after 30s` / failClosed host line is then a *separate, unreproduced* event. Binding them as one mechanism aims the design at the wrong failure.

**Disposition.** Drop "anything that moves HEAD inherits the 48–57s cold path inside the hook." Split: (a) discontinuous HEAD ⇒ deny + cold re-arm via a non-Write channel; (b) forward HEAD ⇒ rebind, writes continue; (c) the 30s host kill remains unexplained and must be reproduced or left as residual. Do not bind fail-open-on-timeout or a larger deposit timeout as the merge fix.

## 2. The 11s is not "the full gated ritual" and not the live probe `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** Gated verify force-reruns only `agent_hooks`. Doctor and `cache_fresh` reuse a green record (`verify-session-ritual-branches.test.ts` "reruns non-deferrable agent-hook readiness while reusing doctor and cache steps"; loop skips any passing step except `agent_hooks`).

My Write probes rewrote that step's `ts` to `2026-08-25T20:34:36Z` — the skip *re-executes and rewrites state*, it does not spawn four-host fixtures.

Reproduced, ghx off PATH, same SHA, same payloads as the issue (method-reconciliation). Concurrent panel load on this worktree, so not a clean control; order of magnitude only:

| Probe | This run | Issue / triage (ghx off) |
|---|---|---|
| Write `tool.before` | 5.9s / 7.7s / 9.6s → `write-ready` | 11.3–11.6s |
| Task `tool.before` | 11.4s → `spawn-ready` | 9.3s |
| Shell `tool.before` | 0.54s / 0.56s → `shell-op-unclassifiable` | 0.5s |
| Read `tool.before` (no ritual) | 0.60s → `not-direct-write` | — |
| `verify:session-ritual --tier=gated` | 6.7s, exit 0 | 8.0–8.9s |

Read vs Write isolates the mutation stack at ~5–11s after ~0.6s boot. I do not refute the issue's warm-path *cost*. I refute the attribution.

Consumers are a different function. The live probe's own ceiling is 24s (4 hosts × 2 fixtures × 1.5s × one retry, `agent-hook-readiness.md` / `LIVE_PROBE_CASE_*`). Nested hosts deposit `timeout: 5` and no `failClosed` (`NESTED_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`). "Consumers run the same deposit with the same timeout" is false.

**Failure mode.** Remedies that only cache or bound the live probe will not remove the dogfood 11s (the probe is already skipped here). An SLO or write-tax table built from these numbers will understate consumer probe cost and overstate "the ritual" as doctor+cache+live.

**Disposition.** State two cost objects: (1) dogfood per-write `verifySessionRitual` after a skip, plus occupancy/scope/active-CLI; (2) consumer live probe, unmeasured on this thread, bounded at 24s. Delete "full gated ritual." Do not bind the 20/50/100-write table as consumer wall time.

## 3. The four directions are not four designs `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** Directions 1 and 2 are the same cut — stop re-deriving readiness on `tool.before` — with different homes for the remaining probe. Direction 4 is already the 24s fixture ceiling; it does not explain the skip-path 11s and does not change failClosed-on-host-kill. Direction 3 (whole-hook fail-open on timeout) is orthogonal and unsafe (lens below).

The cheap checks direction 2 wants — occupancy, scope, intent ceiling, write fence, authz — already run *after* the expensive prefix in `inspectMutationGates`. `session.start` is the wrong home as the deposit exists today: non-blocking, 5s, and the contract says cold `session:start` does *not* run the live probe (`agent-hook-readiness.md` "Mutation-path wiring").

Existing split, already written:

- `inspectSessionRitual` — "A PreToolUse decision must be a probe, not a hidden `doctor` / cache-refresh mutation boundary."
- `verifySessionRitual` — force-reruns `agent_hooks` so "registration/shim drift cannot remain hidden behind an earlier green ritual record."
- `session:ready` — inspect first; verify for doctor/cache; `forceGatedSteps: ["agent_hooks"]` once (`session-ready.ts`).

The dispatcher ignored the inspect docstring and always verifies.

**Failure mode.** Treating the four bullets as a menu hides the real fork (what must be true *for this write* vs *for the session*) and offers an already-landed bound as if it were new. A pick-one vote can land a non-design.

**Disposition.** Recast as two axes, then pick:

1. **Authorization vs readiness.** Per-write: `inspectSessionRitual` (HEAD / worktree / age / persisted gated ok) + occupancy / scope / intent / fence. Per-session: four-host live probe on `session:ready` / compact / first mutation, with a cheap invalidation key (hooks.json mtime, shim mtime, `hostHooks` hash) if drift must still fail closed. That is inventory, not a new engine.

## Injection / swarm lens

Fires: this is a fail-closed authorization path shared by concurrent workers, touching shared state (`xbrief/active/`) and a network dependency.

- **Cross-worker coupling through a shared folder.** Every worker's write authorization depends on the full contents of `xbrief/active/` and on sort order. One worker activating a brief whose origin is stale changes the latency, and potentially the verdict, for every other worker in the repository. A cohort of N workers each triggers the full candidate scan on every write.
- **Third-party control of a local gate.** Anyone who can comment on a linked GitHub issue moves `updated_at`. Combined with the OR-fold, an outside party can flip the whole repository's write gate closed by commenting on the sole active brief's origin issue. I confirmed comments drive `updated_at`: for #3599 and #3611, `updated_at` equals the last comment's `created_at` to the second. That is a low-severity availability lever, not a privilege escalation — no untrusted content is executed, and the failure is denial — but it is an external input on a local authorization path.
- **Contention amplification.** Under N concurrent workers the forge call contends for the same rate-limit bucket and the same process-spawn capacity, which is the most plausible explanation for the spread between the standalone `ghx` timings here and the in-hook figure in 5429413263.
- **No new surface** is introduced by any of the three placements under discussion; the cached-read option strictly reduces this lens's exposure.

## Method reconciliation

Round 2 (5429413263) measured the origin call at **5,860 ms** inside the hook via a `spawnSync` preload; I measured `ghx` standalone at 1,810-3,350 ms and the whole `evaluate()` at 2,505-2,910 ms. I do not read this as a refutation. Their number is the child's full lifetime measured under contention with five concurrent git children and a cold proxy; mine is a warm, uncontended, single-child measurement from a quiet shell. Both land the same conclusion — the forge call is the single largest term on the path and is between 500x and 1,000x the cost of the local alternative in finding 5. My own end-to-end `deft-hook --host cursor --event tool.before` runs on a synthetic `Write` payload returned `{"permission":"allow","code":"write-ready"}` at **10,259 / 14,488 / 12,062 ms** — above the round-1 11 s reading, below the round-2 18 s and the 21,993 ms in 5429307702, and above 5 s in every run while below 30 s in every run. The wall-time spread across five observers is itself the issue body's argument for not gating on wall time, and it holds.

## Road not taken

I considered arguing that the whole active-scope inspection should be keyed to the write target — resolve which brief covers the file being written, then check only that brief. It is the semantically correct shape, and it would fix the OR-fold in finding 1 rather than working around it. I did not lean on it because it requires a file-to-brief ownership mapping the tree does not have (`plan.file_scope` exists but `verify:scope-provenance --enforce` is empty-scope only, so coverage is not universal), and because it is a much larger change than #3736's envelope. It belongs on a sibling issue, and finding 1 should be filed as its own defect regardless of what #3736 does about latency.

## Steelman of the position I am arguing against

The strongest form of "leave it and raise the budget": the OR-fold is a bug in `inspectActiveScope`, not a property of origin freshness. Fix the fold — deny when *any* active brief is stale — and the check becomes the real drift guarantee my finding 1 says it is not. Then it is genuinely load-bearing, removing it genuinely opens a gap, and the honest response to a legitimate six-second check is a budget that fits it. On that reading my finding 1 argues for repairing the check, not relocating it.

I think that is wrong on the measurements, for a reason that is itself measured: at a 51.6% base rate and a 43-minute median time-to-stale, an AND-fold would deny nearly every write in this repository nearly all the time, because the dominant driver of `updated_at` is the framework's own commentary on its own issues rather than requirement change. A correct-as-specified version of this check is unusable at this repository's comment cadence. That is the real reason the OR-fold survived unnoticed: it is what keeps the gate open.

**What would flip my verdict.** A measurement showing that `updated_at` advances on these issues *predominantly* through body edits or label changes that reflect requirement change, rather than through comments — I measured only that comments drive it, on three issues. Or evidence that some consumer of `scope.path` downstream of `dispatcher.ts:1268` does treat the selected brief as the authorization subject for the write target, which would make the OR-fold narrower than I have claimed.

**Verdict:** the round-3 fork does not decide this arc. Drift is frequent, the hot path discards it, the guarantee already lives at `xbrief:preflight`, the forge coupling is a #3422 defect independent of latency, the 5-second budget is not on the Cursor write path, and a cached-read placement neither position considered is already shipped in this tree.
